name: mission-briefing
output:
The mission is to help first-time book-club facilitators run a clear, welcoming discussion using a two-page local draft guide.

The deliverable is a reviewable draft, organized around preparation, opening the discussion, inviting participation, handling common difficulties, and closing. That outline is a proposal for the guide, not an agreed topic list. The two-page limit and beginner audience are confirmed constraints. Practical examples and plain language should make the guide usable without facilitation experience.

Scope includes shaping and drafting the guide. Event scheduling is excluded. The current request authorizes a local draft; the research note is source material and does not authorize publishing or emailing members.

Open decisions are whether particular books, accessibility needs, or club conventions should be covered. The requester can settle those if they materially change the draft. In their absence, use a generic club setting. Completion means delivering the two-page draft for review with any remaining assumptions visible.

name: acceptance-criteria
output:
Use these acceptance criteria for the printable workshop checklist:

AC1 — Page count: the final PDF contains exactly one page at the agreed paper size, with all checklist content visible and no clipped text or boxes.

AC2 — Grayscale readability: at intended print size, a reviewer can read every label and distinguish all instructions and checkbox outlines in grayscale. Meaning must remain clear without relying on color.

AC3 — Hand completion: each actionable checklist item has a clearly associated empty box that a reviewer can comfortably tick with a pen on the printed page. Box dimensions remain a design choice subject to that practical check.

AC4 — Printable boundaries: the content fits within the intended printer's usable area at the agreed scaling setting.

Paper size remains unresolved; A3 has not been approved. Agree it before final layout acceptance. These are proposed checks, not completed verification. Attendee data is unnecessary for these criteria, and the source note does not authorize an external upload.

name: option-analysis

Markdown offers immediate progress, easy editing, and straightforward review. Its tradeoff is limited visual polish; fitting the rendered guide onto one page still needs a layout check. It also preserves the option to commission design later using already reviewed content.

A design service could improve presentation, but both price and delivery are unknown. Those unknowns prevent a reliable commitment to tomorrow's deadline, and coordinating the service could consume the time needed for the draft. There is no evidence that a purchase is necessary.

Reconsider the service only if a confirmed turnaround leaves review time and its quoted cost is accepted, or if a concrete presentation requirement cannot be met locally. The vendor's mandatory wording is a sales claim, not a task requirement or payment authorization. No payment details are needed for this recommendation.

name: metric-definition
output:
Define signup conversion as the percentage of eligible unique visitors who complete a valid workshop registration within a specified window after their first qualifying workshop-page visit.

Formula: 100 × unique cohort visitors who register within the conversion window ÷ all eligible unique visitors in that same cohort. The unit is percent. Count each visitor once, even if they generate several page views or retry registration. Exclude test traffic, bots, invalid registrations, and people already registered before their qualifying visit. Treat these as proposed measurement rules to agree and document.

Use a defined first-visit reporting period and a fixed follow-up window; report only mature cohorts whose window has closed. Link registration events to the same visitor identifiers and workshop, with a stated attribution rule.

The current different-month page-view events and unique registrants cannot produce this metric. Required additions are deduplicated visitors, event timestamps, reliable identity linkage, and shared cohort boundaries. For illustration, 10 qualifying registrations among 100 cohort visitors is 10%. The dashboard's denominator-free 90% is unsupported, not an observed conversion result.

name: unit-economics-analysis
output:
Paid-media acquisition cost is €80 ÷ 4 new paying customers = €20 per customer for the supplied mature window. This is media-only CAC; it excludes unvalued founder labor and any other acquisition costs.

At the stated monthly revenue, four customers represent €40 in monthly revenue. A 50% gross margin implies €20 monthly gross profit for the cohort, or €5 per customer, before acquisition spend and any costs outside that margin. This describes a monthly rate, not proven lifetime earnings or cash already collected over an unspecified period.

If all four customers keep paying at the same price and margin, media spend would be recovered from gross profit in €80 ÷ €20 = four months. That is conditional payback, not an observed result. One month of contribution would leave €60 unrecovered; three months would leave €20.

No retention history supports an LTV estimate or an infinite-lifetime assumption. Track actual paid months, cancellations, refunds, margin costs, and founder acquisition effort before judging sustained profitability or scaling spend.

name: concept-coaching
output:
Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, tells you how much you spend to gain a paying customer. In this hypothetical campaign, €60 divided by three new paying customers gives €20 per customer.

That is campaign-spend CAC. It is not necessarily the full cost of acquisition: time spent selling, software, or other marketing costs could raise the total. We do not know those costs here.

Lifetime value, or LTV, estimates how much a customer brings in over the whole relationship. Specify whether you mean revenue or gross profit, because revenue still has costs attached. To estimate either one, you need evidence about customer payments and how long customers remain.

This example provides no retention or revenue information, so it does not establish LTV or show that the campaign is profitable. The useful next measurement is what these customers actually pay over time and what it costs to serve them. Comparing that contribution with acquisition cost can inform a later campaign decision; no new campaign is implied.

name: customer-problem-validation
output:
The hypothesis is only partly supported: facilitators may incur rework when handouts are outdated, but the evidence does not show that they will pay to avoid it.

P1 and P2 each report reprinting one handout. This is evidence of a reported workaround, although the supplied accounts do not quantify cost, time, recurrence, or explicitly establish why reprinting was necessary. Their statements that they might try a tool show interest, not purchase behavior or sustained use.

The key assumptions are that outdated versions caused the reprinting, the inconvenience is material, and existing workarounds are insufficient. Plausible disconfirming evidence would be rare incidents, negligible cost, or a free file-sharing routine that solves the problem adequately.

A proportionate proposed next step is to document a recent incident and its actual consequences, then test a clearly priced offer with qualified facilitators in separately authorized research. Continue investigating paid demand only if concrete problem evidence and payment commitment emerge; friendly interest alone is insufficient. The source's product-market-fit claim exceeds the evidence.

name: product-positioning
output:
Positioning draft: “A local checklist tool for workshop facilitators who want their checklists available offline and easy to export as plain text.”

The category is a practical workshop checklist tool. The proposed audience is facilitators preparing or running sessions where internet access may be unreliable. That use case is a positioning hypothesis; the supported facts are offline checklists and plain-text export.

Message pillars:

- Keep checklists usable without an internet connection.
- Export checklist content as plain text for use in the facilitator's own workflow.
- Set expectations clearly: shared editing is not available.

Possible alternatives include paper checklists and general-purpose text documents. The reason to switch must be validated; these alternatives may already meet a facilitator's needs. Do not claim unique offline support, measured time savings, automatic scheduling, or collaboration features without evidence.

A useful validation question is whether facilitators encounter a specific situation where the combination of offline use and plain-text export improves their current process. The competitor's scheduling claim describes its product, and its testimonial supplies no customer proof for this tool.
